title: Structuring the Unstructured - Cedric Clyburn, Red Hat

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is building document processing pipelines that convert unstructured enterprise documents into structured formats for AI systems. Docling is a developer tool used by software builders, with RAG and enterprise document processing as key application areas. The talk covers data preparation through document conversion and system development through RAG pipeline and agent integration construction. Assumes familiarity with RAG, Python, and AI concepts while introducing specific tools and techniques. The session is a live demo with hands-on workshop demonstrations of Docling capabilities. summary: Cedric Clyburn, a Senior Developer Advocate at Red Hat, frames his talk around the central challenge of working with unstructured data in AI applications. He stresses that context is the most important aspect of building AI applications and agents, yet most organizational data exists in unstructured formats—PDFs, presentations, contracts, technical docs, meeting notes, scanned documents, diagrams, tables, and images—that must be transformed into formats LLMs can understand like markdown or JSON. He illustrates the stakes with a viral example: 20 scientific papers adopted a nonsensical term because an AI misinterpreted a scanned PDF, merging two words from different columns, and this term is now cited by other researchers. Clyburn contrasts approaches: simple PDF parsers are fast and cheap but truncate text, merge content incorrectly, lose table structure, and omit images; frontier models produce higher-quality output but are expensive (~$30 per million output tokens), non-deterministic, and inconsistent across versions. Docling, an open-source tool part of the Linux Foundation, is presented as the middle ground: a fast, cheap, local CLI and library that converts various input sources to markdown, JSON, and Pydantic data types using OCR and vision models. A Hugging Face use case showed 50x cost savings compared to VLMs and naive OCR, running on CPU without GPU. Beyond basic conversion, Clyburn demonstrates table extraction (8 tables from a source PDF), image extraction with bounding boxes and layout visualization, PII removal use cases, and vision language model enrichment using a local Granite model via Ollama to generate detailed image descriptions. He introduces chunkless or agentic RAG using Docling's document outline as the retrieval index, eliminating the need for chunkers, embedding models, or vector databases—the LLM iterates over the markdown outline to find relevant sections. He demonstrates this with a Docling paper (20 sections) and the IBM 2025 annual report (418 sections). For scale, Clyburn shows Docling Serve as a REST API microservice deployable via containers or Kubernetes, and the Docling MCP server for AI agent integration with tools like Claude Code and VS Code, providing conversion, generation, and manipulation tools to the agent. He closes by emphasizing Docling's fully local, open-source, no-GPU-required operation and its integration with RAG frameworks and agentic systems.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Context is the most critical aspect of building AI applications and agents, and most enterprise data is locked in unstructured formats that must be transformed for LLM consumption.

Docling is an open-source, local CLI and library (part of the Linux Foundation) that converts unstructured documents to markdown, JSON, and Pydantic formats using OCR and vision models, without needing a GPU.

Chunkless or agentic RAG uses Docling's document outline as the retrieval index, eliminating the need for chunkers, embedding models, or vector databases—the LLM iterates over section summaries to find relevant content.
Docling supports image annotation with vision language models (e.g., local Granite via Ollama) to enrich source images and diagrams with detailed descriptions for stronger RAG pipelines.
Docling Serve enables scaling document processing as a REST API microservice via containers or Kubernetes, handling hundreds or thousands of documents at a time.
The Docling MCP server integrates document processing capabilities into AI agents like Claude Code or Cursor via the Model Context Protocol, offering conversion, generation, and manipulation tools.

Simple PDF parsers truncate text, merge content incorrectly, and lose table structure and images; frontier models are expensive (~$30 per million output tokens), non-deterministic, and inconsistent across versions.
Docling can extract and export tables as data frames, visualize document layout with bounding boxes, and support PII removal from source documents before extraction.
Accurate document processing directly determines whether AI application outputs are correct or hallucinated, as demonstrated by the scientific papers example.
Understand how to extract structure from raw enterprise documents for downstream AI systems like RAG and agents

sections.title: Introduction: The Unstructured Data Challenge
sections.summary: Clyburn introduces himself as a Red Hat open-source engineer and frames the problem: context is critical for AI applications, but most data is in unstructured formats (PDFs, presentations, contracts, technical docs, meeting notes, scanned documents, diagrams, tables, images). He previews the session goal of learning to extract structure from raw enterprise documents for RAG and agents, and introduces Docling as the open-source tool to be covered.

sections.title: Why Advanced Document Processing Matters
sections.summary: Clyburn explains the need for advanced document processing, noting data is the key ingredient for RAG and fine-tuning regardless of model choice. He shares a viral example of 20 scientific papers adopting a nonsensical term because an AI misinterpreted a scanned PDF by merging two words from different columns—demonstrating the real-world consequences of poor document processing.

sections.title: Limitations of Simple Parsers and Frontier Models
sections.summary: Clyburn contrasts simple PDF parsers (fast, cheap, but truncate text, lose table structure, and omit images) with frontier models (high quality but expensive at ~$30 per million output tokens, non-deterministic, and inconsistent across versions). He frames the need for a middle ground solution.

sections.title: Docling: The Open-Source Middle Ground
sections.summary: Clyburn introduces Docling as a fast, cheap, local CLI and library part of the Linux Foundation that converts various input sources to markdown, JSON, and Pydantic formats using OCR and vision models. He notes its use at Red Hat for processing thousands of product documentation PDFs and highlights integrations for local or air-gapped environments.

sections.title: Scale, Cost, and Use Cases
sections.summary: Clyburn shares a public use case from Leandro at Hugging Face showing 50x cost savings with Docling compared to VLMs and naive OCR, running on CPU. He also demonstrates image annotation with vision language models and structured output extraction from invoices (bill number, total invoice price, sender name) as Pydantic data.

sections.title: Live Demo: Basic PDF Conversion with Docling
sections.summary: Clyburn begins the demo using the Docling workshop repository. He shows importing the document converter, converting Docling's own research paper PDF to markdown, and exploring the Pydantic data type to inspect pages, tables, and content. He highlights table extraction and export to a data frame for rendering, emphasizing the value beyond basic text conversion.

sections.title: Image Extraction, Layout Visualization, and VLM Enrichment
sections.summary: Clyburn demonstrates exporting 8 tables from the source PDF ready for RAG applications. He then sets up a PDF pipeline to extract and visualize images, showing picture content with captions and embedded text elements. He uses the layout visualizer with bounding boxes to show all extractable elements (headers, text, subtitles, photos), noting PII removal use cases. He enriches source images using a local Granite model via Ollama to generate detailed image descriptions, enhancing RAG pipeline quality.

sections.title: Chunkless/Agentic RAG with Docling
sections.summary: Clyburn introduces chunkless or agentic RAG using Docling's document outline as the retrieval index, eliminating the need for chunkers, embedding models, or vector databases. The LLM iterates over section summaries to find relevant content. He demonstrates with a Docling paper (20 sections, ~5 iterations) and the larger IBM 2025 annual report (418 sections), asking about Red Hat's revenue growth, showing how the agent iterates to find relevant sections without a vector database.

sections.title: Scaling with Docling Serve and MCP Server
sections.summary: Clyburn addresses scaling to hundreds of thousands of PDFs using Docling Serve as a REST API microservice deployable via containers or Kubernetes, with options for OCR, backend, and image annotation. He then introduces the Docling MCP server for AI agent integration via the Model Context Protocol, connecting tools like Claude Code and VS Code. The MCP server provides conversion, generation, and manipulation tools to the agent, enabling agentic document processing without manual argument specification.

sections.title: Wrap-Up and Conclusion
sections.summary: Clyburn summarizes Docling's capabilities: fully local PDF-to-markdown/JSON conversion without GPU, fast, cheap, and open-source. He describes the backend pipelines using OCR and layout analysis to produce Pydantic Docling documents exportable to multiple formats, with HybridChunker for chunking and integrations with RAG frameworks and agentic systems. He thanks the AI engineering team, encourages trying Docling, and invites connections on LinkedIn.
